items.answer: Immersion in virtual reality (VR) means that the user's senses are blocked so that the user receives no input from the real-world environment and receives input only from the virtual world.

Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
In 1997, computer-vision techniques were used to overlay augmented reality (AR) content on real-world markers, and tracking was used to register the AR content in three dimensions.
Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.
Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.

An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

questions.question: What is the overall design goal of a virtual reality system?
options: Creating a high degree of photorealism
Creating a high degree of interaction fidelity
Creating a high degree of representational fidelity
Creating a high degree of presence
questions.explanation: The goal of any VR system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning users believe they are in a real world while actually in a virtual one.

questions.question: For a user who treats real-world perception and sensation as the gold standard, what should a VR system do?
options: Match real-world experience as closely as possible
Avoid exact mimicry of the real world
Surpass the user's day-to-day reality
Use only abstract, non-objective environments
questions.explanation: When reality is the gold standard, reality is what is perceived and sensed in the real world, so the VR goal is to match that experience closely.

questions.question: For a user who expects VR reality to go beyond lived day-to-day reality, what is the design goal?
options: Match the real world exactly
Present only familiar real-world places
Surpass the user's idea of reality
Limit the experience to lived day-to-day reality
questions.explanation: For this conception, reality in VR should be beyond or surpassing day-to-day reality, not an exact mimicry of the real world.

questions.question: Why do different conceptions of reality make VR evaluation ambiguous?
options: Because surpassing reality is always easy to comprehend
Because a single fixed definition of reality is universally accepted
Because all users share the same gold standard of reality
Because a system that matches one group's sense of reality may be poor by another group's standard
questions.explanation: Different users define reality differently, so a system can satisfy one group while seeming bad, creepy, or hard to comprehend to another.

data.text: The goal of a virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence. Some people want to match real-world experience as closely as possible, while others want to surpass it. These differing conceptions of reality make the evaluation of a VR system ambiguous.
points: The goal of VR systems is to create a high degree of presence.
Some people want VR to match real-world experience as closely as possible.
Others want VR to surpass their daily reality rather than mimic it.
These differing conceptions of reality make evaluating VR systems ambiguous.

questions.question: Which best describes the uncanny valley effect?
options: Familiarity caused by fully realistic digital humans
Unease caused by almost-human digital figures with subtle imperfections
Comfort caused by clearly non-human virtual objects
Preference caused by abstract virtual environments
questions.explanation: The uncanny valley effect is that digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease or eeriness rather than familiarity because of subtle imperfections.

questions.question: In the uncanny valley plot, how does familiarity change for moving objects as human likeness increases?
options: It falls first, then rises to a peak, then falls again
It falls steadily throughout the range of human likeness
It rises, then falls more sharply to a minimum, then rises again
It rises steadily throughout the range of human likeness
questions.explanation: As an artificial object becomes more human-like, familiarity first increases, then decreases more sharply for moving objects, reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley region, and then increases again.

questions.question: What is the main design implication of the uncanny valley effect for VR content?
options: Use only abstract objects to guarantee a comfortable experience
Always match reality exactly to maximize user familiarity
Avoid all human-like figures in every VR experience
Balance realism because exact human likeness can reduce familiarity
questions.explanation: Trying to match reality exactly may not produce a good VR experience if human-like figures fall in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.

data.text: Digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first. Familiarity with human-like objects first increases, then decreases in the uncanny valley region, typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness, and then increases again. When creating a VR experience, trying to match reality exactly may not produce a good experience if figures fall in the uncanny valley, so there is a trade-off over how much realism to include.
points: Digital representations of humans that appear almost real can evoke unease because of subtle imperfections that may not be readily recognizable at first.
Familiarity with human-like objects first increases, then decreases in the uncanny valley region (typically between 70 and 85 percent human likeness), and then increases again.
There is a trade-off over how much realism to include because matching reality exactly may not produce a good experience if figures fall in the uncanny valley.

activities.title: Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases

items.title: Order the changes in familiarity as human likeness increases
steps: Familiarity increases for moving and stationary objects
Familiarity decreases, more sharply for moving objects
Familiarity reaches a minimum in the uncanny valley
Familiarity increases for highly human-like objects

questions.question: Representational fidelity in a virtual reality experience refers to
options: how familiar the experience is with real or possible Earth places
how closely virtual task actions match real-world task actions
how well the user's experience matches the creator's intended experience
how much photorealism is required for virtual presence
questions.explanation: Representational fidelity is the degree to which a VR experience conveys, matches, or exploits familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth. The other options describe interaction fidelity, experiential fidelity, or a false requirement for photorealism.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of high interaction fidelity?
options: Sitting still and pressing a button to move forward
Presenting purely abstract, non-objective virtual places
Translating intense, realistic physical activities into virtual activities
Letting every user roam freely so each session differs
questions.explanation: High interaction fidelity involves intense realistic physical actions, in which real-world physical activities are translated into virtual activities. Sitting and moving by button press is very low interaction fidelity, while the other options relate to different fidelity concerns.

questions.question: Experiential fidelity in virtual reality describes
options: the degree to which digital humans are perceived as familiar
the match between the user's personal experience and the creator's intended experience
the match between a virtual place and familiar Earth places
the match between virtual physical actions and real-world physical actions
questions.explanation: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. The other options describe interaction fidelity, representational fidelity, or the uncanny valley.

questions.question: Why can a free-roaming virtual world with endless possibilities have low experiential fidelity?
options: It requires users to perform intense physical actions
It can make every usage lead to a different experience
It places real-world constraints on virtual navigation
It makes every usage lead to the same intended experience
questions.explanation: A free-roaming virtual world with endless possibilities can lead every usage to a different experience, which is not what happens in the real world and lowers experiential fidelity. Placing real-world constraints on navigation, movement, and interaction makes the experience closer to the real world.

questions.question: Why should virtual reality developers maintain representational, interaction, and experiential fidelity as high as possible?
options: So every user in a free-roaming world has the same experience
So photorealism or human-like objects become necessary for presence
So the system no longer needs to consider immersion and presence
So the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience
questions.explanation: Developers should maintain the three fidelities to the highest degree possible so that the uncanny valley effect does not affect the virtual world experience. Presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects, and developers should still consider immersion and presence.

data.text: Presence does not require photorealism, but developers should consider representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities. Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual experience conveys familiarity with a place on Earth, while interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for virtual tasks correspond to real-world actions. Finally, experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's experience matches the creator's intent, and maintaining high fidelities helps ensure the uncanny valley effect does not affect the experience.
points: Presence does not require photorealism, but developers should consider representational, interaction, and experiential fidelities.
Representational fidelity is the degree to which a virtual experience conveys familiarity with a place that is or could be on Earth.
Interaction fidelity is the degree to which physical actions for virtual tasks correspond to equivalent real-world actions.
Experiential fidelity is the degree to which a user's experience matches the creator's intended experience.
Developers should maintain high fidelities to ensure the uncanny valley effect does not affect the experience.

questions.question: Why are the main challenges of AR systems described as mostly technological rather than psychological?
options: Because immersion is not a major concern in AR and psychological effects are less important than in VR.
Because AR depends only on the user's sense of presence in a virtual world.
Because AR removes the need for display and interaction technology.
Because psychological effects are stronger in AR than in VR.
questions.explanation: The segment states that AR challenges are mostly technological because immersion is not a major concern and psychological effects are less important in AR than in VR.

questions.question: Why is suitable display technology needed to combine real and virtual content in AR?
options: To replace the real-world representation with a fully virtual scene.
To determine the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor.
To overlay virtual content on the device's representation of the real world.
To provide the only possible input modality for real-time interaction.
questions.explanation: Combining real and virtual content in AR requires display technology that can overlay virtual content on the representation of the real world on the device.

questions.question: What does real-time interaction in AR require?
options: A high degree of immersion to make the experience psychologically convincing.
A complete virtual environment that hides the real-world representation.
Only a display that overlays virtual content without user input.
Suitable input devices and input modalities for interacting with overlaid virtual content.
questions.explanation: Real-time interaction in AR requires suitable forms of interaction, including input devices and input modalities, so the user can interact with digital content overlaid on the real world.

questions.question: What does three-dimensional registration mean in an AR system?
options: Showing virtual content on a screen without aligning it to real-world objects.
Replacing real-world objects with virtual objects in a virtual environment.
Recording the user's eye movements to estimate where they are looking.
Anchoring virtual content in the real world so it appears part of the physical environment.
questions.explanation: 3D registration in AR means anchoring virtual content at a suitable place in the real world so that it appears to be part of the physical environment and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects.

questions.question: What role does pose determination play in AR registration and tracking?
options: It provides the input devices and modalities needed for real-time interaction.
It removes the need to align virtual content with the physical environment.
It establishes the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor and updates that pose as the user moves.
It selects the display technology used to overlay virtual content on the real world.
questions.explanation: Pose means the viewer's position and orientation relative to a real-world anchor. Conceptually, pose determination includes a registration phase that sets the initial pose and a tracking phase that updates it as the user moves.

data.text: AR challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological because psychological effects are less important than in VR. AR requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the real world and suitable interaction modalities for users. Furthermore, 3D registration anchors virtual content in the real world through pose determination, which consists of both a registration phase and a tracking phase.
points: AR challenges are mostly technological rather than psychological.
AR requires suitable display technology to overlay virtual content on the real world.
Real-time interaction requires suitable forms of interaction and input devices.
3D registration anchors virtual content in the real world so it mixes seamlessly.
Pose determination includes both a registration phase and a tracking phase.

questions.question: In virtual reality systems, which major concept is tied to psychological issues?
options: Presence
Representational fidelity
Tracking
Immersion
questions.explanation: VR concerns include technological and psychological issues; technological issues are tied to immersion, while psychological issues are tied to presence.

questions.question: What does the uncanny valley effect in virtual reality refer to?
options: Uneasiness caused by using virtual input actions that do not match real-world task actions
Uneasiness caused by making augmented reality virtual content difficult to register in the real world
Uneasiness caused by making the virtual environment completely abstract and unfamiliar to real-world experience
Uneasiness caused by making the virtual environment as familiar as possible to real-world experience
questions.explanation: The uncanny valley effect is the uneasiness or creepiness that can occur when a VR environment is made too familiar to the user's real-world experience.

questions.question: Which three fidelities should a virtual reality developer consider to help avoid the uncanny valley effect?
options: Representational fidelity, experiential fidelity, and interaction fidelity
Immersion, presence, and photorealism
Registration fidelity, tracking fidelity, and anchor fidelity
Display fidelity, input fidelity, and tracking fidelity
questions.explanation: To avoid the uncanny valley effect in VR, developers should be aware of representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.

questions.question: The major technological issues in augmented reality consist of which three areas?
options: Display technology, input mechanisms and technology, and pose estimation and updating
Display technology, input mechanisms and technology, and psychological presence
Presence, immersion, and pose estimation and updating
Display technology, representational fidelity, and interaction fidelity
questions.explanation: The major AR issues are mostly technological and consist of proper display technology, proper input mechanisms and technology, and pose estimation and updating, popularly called tracking.

data.text: VR systems are defined by technological immersion and psychological presence. To avoid the uncanny valley effect where familiarity causes uneasiness, developers should be aware of representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity. Conversely, the major issues in augmented reality are mostly technological and consist of display technology, input mechanisms, and tracking.
points: VR systems involve technological immersion and psychological presence.
Making VR environments too familiar can cause the uncanny valley effect of uneasiness.
Avoiding the uncanny valley requires awareness of representational, experiential, and interaction fidelity.
AR issues are mostly technological, involving display, input mechanisms, and tracking.

questions.question: Why can increasing photorealism in a virtual reality system reduce rather than improve the user's sense of presence?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality system aims to create presence, and the closer it is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides. Presence does not require photorealism or human-like objects. The uncanny valley effect shows that almost-real digital representations can evoke unease, so making figures more human-like creates a trade-off over how much realism to include.

questions.question: How can representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity help a virtual reality system avoid the uncanny valley effect?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality system developer should consider representational fidelity, interaction fidelity, and experiential fidelity along with immersion and presence. Maintaining these fidelities helps keep the uncanny valley effect from affecting the virtual world experience. This is important because making environments as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience can cause uneasiness or creepiness.

questions.question: Why are the major issues in augmented reality systems described as mostly technological, whereas virtual reality systems also raise psychological concerns?
questions.reference_answer: Augmented reality challenges are mostly technological because immersion is not a major concern and psychological effects are less important in augmented reality than in virtual reality. The major augmented reality issues are proper display technology, proper input mechanisms, and pose estimation and updating, which is popularly called tracking. In virtual reality, the two major concerns are technological and psychological, leading to immersion and presence.

questions.question: Why is pose determination essential for three-dimensional registration in augmented reality, and how do the registration and tracking phases differ?
questions.reference_answer: Three-dimensional registration anchors virtual content in the real world at a suitable place so that it appears to mix seamlessly with physical objects. To do this, the viewer's position and orientation relative to an anchor must be determined. Conceptually, the registration phase determines that pose at the start, while the tracking phase updates the pose as the user moves. Earlier augmented reality systems used tracking to register content in three dimensions by overlaying it on real-world markers.
